title: Whats the Story PISA Glory
author: Chris Reid
summary: Chris Reid, an English secondary teacher who has been critical of his country's post-2010 reforms, responds to Daisy Christodoulou's puzzlement that nobody else is celebrating England's PISA 2025 results. He concedes that the test scores are real and that the knowledge-rich curriculum and related reforms probably deserve some credit. He then turns to the PISA pupil questionnaire, where England sits near the bottom of the OECD on life satisfaction, school belonging and bullying, and has more reported disorder in science lessons than the OECD average. He notes that England's climb in the rankings owes much to holding steady while other systems slid, and that the Scotland comparison is muddied by differences in exams, league tables and test timing. Estonia, which beats England on both attainment and wellbeing, is offered as proof that the two goals need not be traded off. His conclusion is that England must work out what drove the gains and then keep them while making school a place pupils feel they belong.
points: England's PISA rise is mostly a matter of holding steady while much of the developed world fell, not of large score gains, which is the frame Reid wants readers to keep in mind.
The questionnaire data show high attainment alongside bottom-ten results for belonging (70% against an OECD 76%) and bullying, so a single headline rank hides a split picture.
Estonia outscores England in science while also beating it on life satisfaction and calm lessons, which undercuts any assumption that academic strength must cost pupil wellbeing.
Reid models a useful habit for education debate: he admits his own ambivalence and partial error rather than defending a camp.
The proposed agenda is two questions, what actually drove the gains and how to keep them while fixing belonging, rather than a verdict for or against the reforms.
quotes: In truth, England’s scores haven’t actually risen much. Science (516) is about where it was in 2015 (512). Same story in maths (492 now, 493 then) and reading (497 now, 500 then).

Alongside that, though, English 15-year-olds rate their life satisfaction at 6.7 out of 10, against an OECD average of 7.3. That puts England joint last of the 32 OECD countries that asked. Fewer than a quarter of English teenagers rate their life 9 or 10, against more than a third across the OECD.

Only 70% feel they belong at school, against an OECD average of 76%: 33rd of 38. Bullying is more common than in most OECD countries: where 1 st is least bullied, England is 32nd of 38, based on how often pupils say they’ve been made fun of, threatened, hit or pushed, had nasty rumours spread about them or had upsetting things posted about them online in the past year. 2
The relationships are there; the connection to school isn’t. And I’ve seen it play out, day after day, year after year. Those kids who just drop off the radar.

Do you have to trade attainment for satisfied pupils? Estonia suggests not. It beats England on science (527 to 516), life satisfaction (7.4 to 6.7), belonging (80% to 70%) and calm lessons (24% report regular noise and disorder, against 39%).
If ‘top ten for science’ tells us something meaningful about the impact of England’s educational changes then so does ‘bottom ten for belonging’.

When the results came out, I should have been celebrating. Instead, I was ambivalent. Deep down, I didn’t believe the changes had been positive, and yet the scores were complicating the picture I held.
Because two things are becoming clear. In England, something is working: policy reforms might well hold the clues. And in England, something is going badly wrong.
